messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun has been a potter for over fifty years, but now, at seventy-five, his hands tremble for reasons that have nothing to do with age. It was his wife, Sitara, who finally made the call, her voice tight with a concern he could no longer deflect. For decades, the past was a country he had left behind, a sealed border in his mind. But in the last few years, the border has dissolved. The story he has never been able to tell in words now lives in his body, speaking through the sudden rigidity of his spine and the frantic darting of his eyes. The memories of his family’s flight from their village are not a narrative but a series of sensory shards: the low, grinding rumble of a truck engine, the blinding glare of the sun off a soldier’s rifle, the smell of dust and fear, and the sight of hastily covered mounds of earth by the roadside. These flashes feel more real to him than the memory of his own wedding day, arriving without warning and leaving him breathless and disoriented in his own sun-drenched studio. Because these sensory fragments feel so immediate and real, his senses have become finely tuned to any echo of them in the present; the rumble of a distant engine is no longer just background noise, and the glint of sun on a passing car can stop him in his tracks.

The intrusive, wordless nature of these memories has reshaped his world. Believing he is fundamentally unable to handle even the slightest upset, the fragments of the past have taught him that safety lies in absolute control of his environment. He spends hours at the large window of his studio, not admiring the street, but scanning it, a self-appointed watchman guarding against a threat only he can perceive. This constant scanning has trained his senses to be exquisitely sensitive, turning previously neutral sounds like a truck's engine or the glint of sun on a car into potent alarms. The sight of a police car cruising down the block is no longer an ordinary event; it is a confirmation of his deepest fear that danger is ever-present and he must remain on high alert. This sense of imminent threat has bled into his perception of himself, reinforcing a devastating belief that he is no longer the capable man who built a life and a business from nothing. He feels brittle, convinced that any unexpected event, even a happy one, could shatter him.

This cycle of fear and vigilance feeds itself relentlessly. His conviction that he must always be on guard makes him hyper-aware of his surroundings, which in turn makes him more likely to notice the very things that torment him. The sound of a car backfiring sends a jolt of terror through him, not just a startling noise but an echo of a gunshot from a past he cannot articulate. This immediate threat perception validates his belief that he is right to be so careful, that the world is indeed a minefield. The memories themselves are also shaped by this pervasive sense of inadequacy; when he feels most weak and incapable, the fragmented images return with greater force, their vividness a testament to his powerlessness. It is in those moments that he feels most certain he cannot cope, that the past has finally defeated him.

Over the last year, these patterns have hardened into rigid rules for living. He has started avoiding any situation that might hold a hint of confrontation, deferring to his wife on every small decision and refusing to discuss his increasingly withdrawn behaviour. This avoidance, meant to protect him, only deepens his sense of being incapable. More painfully, he has begun to retreat from joy. He declined to attend his grand-nephew's first birthday party, terrified of the noise and the crowd. He recently learned of the death of an old friend and could not bring himself to go to the funeral, the very idea of a cemetery bringing forth unbearable, silent images of those roadside graves. Each event he avoids serves as fresh evidence of his own fragility, tightening the loop of anxiety. His world has shrunk to his home and his studio, and now even the studio, once his sanctuary, feels like a cage.

He sought therapy because he found himself unable to work. The clay felt foreign in his hands, his focus shattered by the need to scan the street, to listen for approaching engines. The craft that had defined his identity, that had been his anchor in a new country, was slipping away. He told his wife he felt like a ghost, haunting the edges of his own life. What he hopes for, he explained quietly, is not to forget, but to feel solid again, to be able to sit at his wheel and feel the spin of the clay without the world spinning away from him.
